title: Production Hosting: Build, Environment, Deep Links, and Rollback
description: Prepare a Vite SPA for production and verify routing, configuration, and recovery in a deployed preview.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish dev server, production build and deployment.
Explain generated dist assets, content hashes and build-time client configuration.
Separate public browser configuration from server secrets.
Resolve Vite mode-specific env values without committing local secrets.
Verify direct-route refresh and provider-specific SPA fallback.
Plan preview, smoke tests, monitoring and rollback.

blocks.text: A production release is a pipeline

Running on a development server is not production evidence. A reliable release starts from a reproducible dependency install, runs quality gates, builds static assets, uses correct environment configuration, tests the deployed preview, and preserves a recovery path. Direct URL loads and refresh can behave differently from clicking a link after the app is loaded.

blocks.code:
Clean checkout
  -> npm ci
  -> lint + typecheck + tests
  -> npm run build
  -> deploy preview
  -> verify routes, assets and env config
  -> test critical user journeys
  -> promote release
  -> monitor and rollback if needed

steps.title: Install reproducibly and run quality gates
steps.explanation: CI should use the committed lockfile and run the project's actual quality scripts. Verify script names rather than assuming an example matches every repository.

steps.title: Validate the hosted preview
steps.explanation: Check direct loads and refresh on nested paths, assets, forms and request states. A dev server may hide missing SPA fallback configuration.

steps.title: Release with recovery in mind
steps.explanation: Keep a known-good deployment and define who can roll back plus observable rollback triggers.

blocks.text: Vite variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to browser code and can be recovered from the built bundle. Put public values such as an API base URL there, never a private key or database password. Configure the host to return the SPA entry document for app routes while still serving real assets and API responses correctly.

blocks.title: Client configuration is public
blocks.text: Anything shipped to the browser must be treated as public. Keep secrets in a server-side runtime or deployment secret store. A frontend guard does not authorize access to protected data.

blocks.prompt: Which value is appropriate for a Vite variable prefixed with VITE_?

options.feedback: Client-exposed values can be read from the browser bundle.
A public base URL can be browser configuration; privileged credentials must stay server-side.
Signing keys must never be shipped in client JavaScript.

options.text: A secret whose variable name is obfuscated
options.feedback: Renaming a client variable does not make its value secret.

blocks.explanation: Classify values by whether the browser must receive them, not by the variable name.

blocks.title: Create a deployment smoke-test and rollback plan
blocks.context: Prepare a release that another developer can verify in the hosting preview.
instructions: List clean install, lint, typecheck, tests and production-build gates.
Classify configuration values as public browser values or server secrets.
Test a direct nested route load and refresh in the deployed preview.
Verify assets, forms, request states, keyboard use and narrow layouts.
Define monitoring evidence, rollback owner and an observable trigger.
requirements: The tested commit and build are recorded.
No privileged secret is exposed to browser code.
Direct deep links are tested in the hosted environment.
Smoke tests cover critical user journeys.
A rollback path is specific and actionable.

Client-exposed variables are public; keep credentials server-side.
Test direct URLs, assets, critical journeys and recovery in the deployed environment.

blocks.text: Vite compiles your source into static output under dist/; the host serves those generated files, not your source tree or the development server. Asset filenames commonly include a content hash. When file bytes change, the filename changes, allowing caches to keep an unchanged asset while new HTML refers to the updated one. Treat dist as generated output: inspect it to diagnose a build, but do not hand-edit it or commit it as source. Values used by browser code are substituted at build time, so changing a hosting dashboard value does not rewrite an existing bundle; run a new build and deploy.

blocks.code:
src/main.tsx + src/styles.css
  -> npm run build
  -> dist/index.html
     dist/assets/index-A1B2.js
     dist/assets/index-C3D4.css
  -> CDN caches assets by content hash
  -> changed source produces new asset names

steps.title: Build from source
steps.explanation: The production build compiles and bundles your app. A working dev server does not prove this production transformation succeeds.

steps.title: Inspect the publish output
steps.explanation: dist contains the deployable HTML entry and generated assets. Confirm the host publishes the directory your build actually produces.

steps.title: Reason about caching
steps.explanation: Hashed filenames distinguish changed content. If a page references missing old assets, check deploy consistency and cache behavior instead of renaming generated files manually.

blocks.text: Vite env files: mode and precedence

Vite loads .env and .env.local, plus mode-specific .env.[mode] and .env.[mode].local files. For a key in files, precedence is .env.[mode].local, then .env.[mode], then .env.local, then .env; a value already present in the process environment takes precedence over all loaded files. npm run dev uses development mode by default; npm run build uses production mode. Keep personal .local files out of Git and commit a placeholder-only .env.example. Any VITE_ value included in client code is public. Hosting variables are supplied to the build process; changing them requires a new build of the static bundle.

blocks.code:
# .env
VITE_API_ORIGIN=https://api.example.test

# .env.production
VITE_API_ORIGIN=https://api.example.com

# .env.production.local (ignored by Git)
VITE_API_ORIGIN=https://staging-api.example.net

npm run build  # production mode

steps.title: Resolve the mode-specific value
steps.explanation: For a production build, .env.production.local is the most specific file shown and wins over .env.production and .env. A value exported in the build process environment wins over file values.

steps.title: Check the effective client config
steps.explanation: Verify the intended public API origin in a preview. Do not print secrets in logs; client-exposed VITE_ values are not secret storage.

blocks.text: Provider settings and SPA fallback are not interchangeable

A Git-connected host typically installs dependencies, runs the configured build, publishes dist, and creates preview deploys for branches or pull requests. A manual upload can be useful for a quick experiment, but it does not rebuild on later commits. Vercel and Netlify can both host a Vite SPA; verify the actual build command, output directory, environment scope (preview versus production), and rewrite behavior in current project settings. A common Netlify SPA rule is `/* /index.html 200` in public/_redirects. Scope and test fallbacks so API endpoints and missing asset paths are not accidentally served as the app HTML. Follow current provider docs instead of copying old dashboard screenshots.

blocks.title: Isolate the failing layer before changing settings
blocks.text: A build error belongs in deploy logs; a nested-route 404 points to hosting rewrites; a blank page may come from a JavaScript exception or a missing hashed asset; a failed API request may be a wrong build-time URL, CORS, or backend authorization. Reproduce the deployed URL, inspect DevTools Console and Network, then compare the deployed commit and environment scope. The same symptom can have different causes, so use the response status and request URL as evidence.

blocks.prompt: A preview still calls the production API after you changed a host variable. What should you check first?

options.text: The static client value was embedded in the existing build; rebuild the preview with the intended environment scope
options.feedback: Vite substitutes client environment values during build. Updating a dashboard value does not rewrite already-generated JavaScript.

options.text: The browser needs a server secret before it can read the new value
options.feedback: VITE_ values are public client configuration; privileged secrets must remain server-side.

options.text: Edit the generated dist JavaScript manually
options.feedback: dist is generated output. Correct the build environment and create a new deployment.

options.text: A successful local dev server guarantees the preview used the same mode
options.feedback: Development and production builds use different modes and may receive different environment values.

blocks.explanation: Trace the value from the hosting environment scope into the build job and then into the emitted client bundle.

blocks.title: Diagnose a preview that works locally but fails after deployment
blocks.context: A Vite SPA builds successfully in CI, but its preview calls the wrong API and refreshing /account/settings returns 404.
instructions: Identify which build mode and environment scope the preview build used; explain why changing a host setting requires a rebuild.
Write the Vite env-file precedence and include the higher priority of pre-existing process variables.
Choose a provider-specific fallback check without hiding API or missing-asset errors.
Give an investigation order using DevTools Network/Console and deploy logs; record the deployed commit and build.
Define an observable rollback trigger and a recovery step that restores a known-good deployment.
requirements: Separates build-time public config from runtime server secrets.
Tests a nested route by direct load and refresh.
Does not recommend committing local env files or editing dist by hand.
Uses status codes and request URLs to distinguish a route rewrite from an API/config failure.
Connects rollback to an identified release.
